title: White House Bans Some News Reporters
summary:
Imagine you're a reporter. Your job is to ask questions and tell people what's happening. But one day, you show up to work and they say, "You can't come in anymore."

That's what happened to reporters from three news companies: CNN, Politico, and MS NOW. On Friday, President Donald Trump said he was banning them from the White House. He accused them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration.

On Saturday morning, reporters from these outlets were stopped at the White House. Their press badges — special passes that let them enter — were taken away or turned off. CNN reporter Betsy Klein said a Secret Service agent told her that her badge was deactivated. Politico said its reporter Cheyenne Haslett was denied entry and had her pass revoked.

The news companies are not happy. They say the ban violates their First Amendment rights. The First Amendment is part of the U.S. Constitution that protects freedom of speech and freedom of the press. MS NOW said the White House "belongs to the American people." CNN called the ban "an illegal assault on this fundamental right."

Trump didn't mention specific stories that made him angry. He said it was "just cumulative stories over the last few years." He also said "there may be others to join them."

A group called the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press said the ban is "flatly unconstitutional" and expects courts to strike it down. The White House hasn't said what happens next.
why_it_matters: If reporters can be kept out of the places where leaders work, kids and families get less news about what the government is doing — and that is exactly the kind of thing the First Amendment was written to prevent.

background_read: The First Amendment is part of the Bill of Rights, which was added to the U.S. Constitution in 1791, and it says the government may not stop people from speaking or from printing the news.
Reporters who cover the White House carry special passes and sit in assigned seats in the press briefing room, where presidents answer their questions.
In 2018, the White House took away CNN reporter Jim Acosta's press pass, and a judge ordered that it be given back — a reminder that judges often end up deciding fights like this.

CNN (a big American TV news company), Politico (a news website and newspaper about politics), and the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press (a group of lawyers who defend journalists) are all part of this story.
Article_Structure: WHO: Reporters from CNN, Politico, and MS NOW, President Donald Trump, and a Secret Service agent
WHAT: The White House banned those reporters and turned off or took away their press badges
WHERE: The White House in Washington, D.C., starting on Friday and Saturday
WHY: The President says the outlets wrote "fiction or lies"; the news companies say the ban breaks the First Amendment's promise of a free press

perspectives.description: It says it can decide who enters the building and that the outlets have written stories it calls "fiction or lies," so their reporters are no longer welcome.
They say being shut out is an attack on the freedom of the press, because reporters cannot ask questions or check facts if they are not allowed inside.
They note that judges have stepped into fights over press passes before; the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press expects a court to throw this ban out.
